flawed_step: The claim that quicksort takes O(n log n) on every input, and that sorted input is a cheap case. With the first element as pivot, a sorted array gives the most unbalanced split possible at every level.
counterexample: For each n, take A_n = [1, 2, ..., n], which is already sorted. Trace: the pivot is A[lo] = 1. Lomuto partition compares the pivot with each of the other n-1 elements. None is smaller, so the pivot stays at position lo. That leaves an empty left subarray and a right subarray [2, ..., n] of size n-1, which is still sorted. By induction, C(n) = (n-1) + C(n-1) with C(1) = C(0) = 0, so C(n) = n(n-1)/2. Example: n = 4 gives 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 comparisons. Since n(n-1)/2 divided by n log n goes to infinity, this is Theta(n^2), not O(n log n).
assessment_summary: The statement is false. With a first-element pivot and Lomuto partition, the sorted array [1..n] splits into sizes 0 and n-1 at every step, giving exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is Theta(n^2). How many swaps happen doesn't matter, because running time is defined as the number of comparisons.
